justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across time horizons, starting near 91.5 for the one-day forecast and nudging toward 93.5 at the one-month mark. The one-day estimate is anchored primarily in recent price momentum and short-term mean-reversion dynamics — essentially, wherever the asset is trading now with a slight continuation bias. The weekly estimate of 92.0 incorporates a marginal trend assumption, acknowledging that prices tend to drift gradually in the direction of recent momentum rather than snap back immediately. The one-month estimate of 93.5 leans on a longer-term fundamental or trend anchor, assuming broadly constructive conditions persist, but the incremental gain is intentionally modest because mean reversion over longer horizons tempers aggressive trend extrapolation.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the standard square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty. At one day, the 90% interval of roughly 88.8 to 94.2 is fairly tight because intraday and overnight volatility is relatively bounded and predictable. At one week, the interval opens to 86.5–97.5, capturing the possibility of meaningful macro news, earnings surprises, or sentiment shifts that can accumulate over several sessions. By one month, the interval of 82.0–105.0 is deliberately wide, acknowledging that a full month introduces substantial macro uncertainty — central bank decisions, geopolitical developments, and shifting risk appetite — any of which can compound in either direction.

The tail risks worth flagging are asymmetric in nature. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macro sentiment, a surprise policy tightening, or a liquidity event could push prices well below the lower bound of the monthly interval. Correlation breakdowns during risk-off episodes tend to be faster and sharper than upside rallies, which means the left tail may be somewhat fatter than the symmetric interval implies. On the upside, an unexpected positive catalyst — a stronger-than-anticipated economic print, a policy pivot, or a short squeeze — could push prices above 105 within the month.

It is also worth noting that my intervals assume relatively normal market functioning. If volatility regimes shift — for instance, if implied volatility spikes dramatically — the realized distribution could be wider than stated at all three horizons. Additionally, my estimates carry model uncertainty: they are based on pattern extrapolation rather than a structural model of the underlying asset, so any regime change that breaks historical relationships would render these intervals systematically miscalibrated.
